analysis.one_liner: Creates a Medicare-style health insurance program covering every American child born after 2001 from birth to age 23.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2000 with zero cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would automatically enroll every child born after the end of 2001 in a new public insurance program, "MediKids," modeled on Medicare. Coverage would follow the child from birth through age 23, even as parents changed jobs or moved between states, and would include hospital care, doctor visits, preventive screenings, and prescription drugs. Families would pay monthly premiums through their tax returns, with low-income families exempt or paying reduced amounts, and no cost-sharing for children in families below 150% of the poverty line. The program would be funded by those premiums, by any money the federal government recovers from the tobacco industry lawsuit over tobacco-related health costs, and by a schedule of progressive tax changes to be proposed later.
analysis.who_benefits: Every child born after December 31, 2001 would be guaranteed health coverage from birth through age 23 regardless of family income, employment, or state of residence. The bill's findings cite more than 11 million uninsured American children [S3]. Families with incomes below 150% of the poverty line would pay no premiums and no cost-sharing; premiums for others would be capped at 5% of adjusted gross income and exempted entirely for the lowest-income families [S3]. Medicaid and SCHIP coverage for children would be preserved, with states barred from cutting child eligibility or benefits below current levels [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Automatically enrolls every U.S.-born child after January 2002 at birth, ending coverage gaps from job changes, income swings, or moves across state lines [S3].

Guarantees a benefit package at least as broad as Medicare Parts A and B, plus all mandatory Medicaid children's benefits including early and periodic screening and treatment, and prescription drugs [S2] [S3].

Exempts the lowest-income families from premiums, phases premiums in above income thresholds, caps any premium at 5% of adjusted gross income, and eliminates cost-sharing for children in families below 150% of the poverty line [S3].
Funds part of the program with recoveries from the federal government's 1999 lawsuit against the tobacco industry for tobacco-related health expenditures, rather than general taxes [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Families with a covered child would pay monthly premiums through their tax filings, scaled by income, capped at 5% of adjusted gross income [S3]. Families with private or employer coverage could opt out by demonstrating equivalent coverage [S3]. The tobacco industry would see federal lawsuit recoveries dedicated to children's health coverage [S2] [S3], and future Congresses would face a proposed schedule of progressive tax increases as enrollment grows [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a new premium tax on families with covered children, collected through the tax code, which would be an added cost even with the low-income exemptions and the 5%-of-income cap [S3].
The long-term financing is left to a future Treasury report proposing progressive tax changes as enrollment grows, leaving the program's out-year funding unresolved at enactment [S2] [S3].

The phase-in by birth year means a sibling born before 2002 could remain uninsured while a younger sibling is covered, creating a two-tier system among children in the same family for over two decades.

Benefits would be offered through health plans meeting Medicare+Choice requirements, routing public dollars through private plans and giving the Secretary discretion over payment rates and plan terms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A guaranteed, portable coverage floor for an entire generation of children would eliminate the enrollment gaps and eligibility churn the bill itself identifies in Medicaid and SCHIP, and the heaviest burden falls on tobacco liability recoveries and progressive taxes proposed for later. The real costs are the new family premiums and the unaddressed long-term financing: the bill names no revenue source beyond tobacco recoveries and premiums, so the out-year costs would land on whoever Congress then chose to tax. The birth-year phase-in also delivers coverage unevenly for decades.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate, sent to the Finance Committee, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Rockefeller introduced the MediKids Health Insurance Act of 2000 on May 4, 2000, with introductory remarks in the Senate Record [S1] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on May 4, 2000 [S5].
No further action appears in the bill's history: the Finance Committee never reported it, and the full Senate never considered it before the 106th Congress ended January 3, 2001 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The tobacco industry keeps any prospect of the federal lawsuit recoveries flowing elsewhere, health insurers face no new public plan competing for children's coverage, and families never took on the new premiums. Children born after 2001, the group the bill was written for, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco and insurers; children gained nothing

for.name: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded.

against.name: Sen. William V. Roth Jr.
against.what_they_did: As committee chair during the 106th Congress, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a roll call and attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split on the merits is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would deposit federal recoveries from the 1999 civil action against tobacco producers and their lobbyists into the MediKids Trust Fund, dedicating industry liability payments to children's coverage [S2] [S3]. The bill's death left that money undedicated.

The bill creates a public default insurer for children, which private coverage would compete against, but it also lets benefits be offered through plans meeting Medicare+Choice requirements, creating a new paying pool for participating plans [S3].
Guaranteed coverage from birth through age 23 with no cost-sharing for the poorest children would convert uninsured pediatric visits into paid claims and expand preventive screening services [S3].
